'''Robert Mark Wightman''' (born July 4, 1947) is an electrochemist and professor emeritus of [[chemistry]] at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]]. He is best known for his work in the areas of [[ultramicroelectrode]]s, [[electrochemistry]], and [[neurochemistry]]. One of Wightman's most notable achievements is the development of the [[ultramicroelectrode]] and microelectrode voltammetry.<ref>[https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/ac00232a004 "Microvoltammetric Electrodes" (PDF). Analytical Chemistry. August 1981.]</ref> At the same time as Wightman's innovations, the microelectrode was developed independently by [[Martin Fleischmann]] at the [[University of Southampton]]. In 2011, Wightman had the 192nd highest h-index, 74, of any living chemist.<ref>[http://www.rsc.org/images/H-index%20ranking%20of%20living%20chemists(December%202011)_tcm18-211414.pdf "H-index ranking of living chemists" (PDF). Chemistry World. 12 December 2011.]</ref> As of 2018, Wightman was an author of over 390 papers and had an [[h-index]] of 103.<ref>[https://www.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=24447604900 "Scopus, Author Details - Wightman, Robert Mark"]</ref>

== Education and academic career ==

=== Education ===
Wightman received his B.A. degree with honors from [[Erskine College]] in [[Due West, South Carolina]] in 1968 and earned a Ph.D. in chemistry from the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] in 1974, where he worked with [[Royce W. Murray|Royce Murray]]. At UNC - Chapel Hill, Wightman began focusing his research on [[electrochemistry]]. Wightman was a [[postdoctoral researcher]] from 1974 to 1976 at the [[University of Kansas]] in [[Lawrence, Kansas]] under the direction of Ralph N. Adams. His work focused on [[electroanalytical methods]] and [[redox]] chemistry.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://imageserve.chem.unc.edu/assets/pdf_files/faculty_cv/wightman/wightman_cv.pdf|title=Curriculum Vitae of Robert Mark Wightman|access-date=April 26, 2018}}</ref>

=== Positions held ===
Wightman worked at [[Indiana University Bloomington]] in [[Bloomington, Indiana]] from 1976 to 1989. He worked as an [[assistant professor]] from 1976 to 1982, and he was promoted to the position of [[associate professor]] in 1982 and later to a full [[professor]] in 1985. He worked as a full professor until 1989 when he took a position at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.<ref name=":0" />

From 1989 to his retirement in 2017, Wightman was the [[William R. Kenan Jr.]] professor of chemistry at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]]. He was appointed to the neurobiology curriculum in 1989 and was given an external faculty position at the [[Neuroscience]] Center at UNC - Chapel Hill in 2004.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Faculty Emeriti |url=https://chem.unc.edu/faculty-emeriti/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=UNC Chapel Hill Department of Chemistry}}</ref>

Wightman also worked as a [[research associate]] at [[Barts and The London School of Medicine and Dentistry|London Hospital Medical College]] at the [[University of London]] in 1984. He was a [[visiting professor]] at [[Duke University]] Medical Center in [[Durham, NC]] in 1997 and at the [[University of Cambridge]] in [[Cambridge, England]] in the [[anatomy]] department in 2004. Wightman was also a [[visiting fellow]] in the [[Churchill College]] at Cambridge in 2011. He has been an advisor for over 100 doctoral students, masters students, postdoctoral associates, and visiting faculty.<ref name=":0" />

Wightman has also been an editor for: Biosensors & Bioelectronics, Analytical Chemistry, Journal of Electroanalytical Chemistry, Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics, 
Synapse, and Annual reviews of Analytical Chemistry.

=== Current research ===
The Wightman research group is primarily interested voltammetric sensors, particularly the [[ultramicroelectrode]]. Their small size allows for analysis and measurements at the level of a single biological cell. By coupling these electrodes to fast-scan voltammetric methods, the group has been able to monitor sub-second changes in concentrations of the [[neurotransmitter]]s [[dopamine]], [[norepinephrine]], and [[serotonin]] in response to pharmacological and electrical stimuli.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kirkpatrick|first1=D. C.|last2=McKinney|first2=C. J.|last3=Manis|first3=P. B.|last4=Wightman|first4=R. M.|date=2016-08-02|title=Expanding neurochemical investigations with multi-modal recording: simultaneous fast-scan cyclic voltammetry, iontophoresis, and patch clamp measurements|journal=The Analyst|language=en|volume=141|issue=16|pages=4902–4911|doi=10.1039/c6an00933f|pmid=27314130|pmc=5134327|bibcode=2016Ana...141.4902K|issn=1364-5528}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bucher|first1=Elizabeth S.|last2=Wightman|first2=R. Mark|date=2015-07-10|title=Electrochemical Analysis of Neurotransmitters|journal=Annual Review of Analytical Chemistry|volume=8|issue=1|pages=239–261|doi=10.1146/annurev-anchem-071114-040426|pmid=25939038|issn=1936-1327|pmc=4728736|bibcode=2015ARAC....8..239B}}</ref>

== Awards and achievements ==
Mark Wightman's awards include but are not limited to:

*2011 - [[Herty Medal]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/89/i16/Herty-Award-Mark-Wightman.html|title=Herty Award To Mark Wightman {{!}} April 18, 2011 Issue - Vol. 89 Issue 16 {{!}} Chemical & Engineering News|website=cen.acs.org|access-date=2018-04-24}}</ref>
*2010 - Sir [[Bernard Katz]] Award
*2008 - [[American Chemical Society]] Award in [[Analytical Chemistry]]
*2006 - Ralph N. Adams Award in Bioanalytical Chemistry
*2002 - [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] Fellow
*1999 - [[Erskine College]] Academic Hall of Fame
*1996 - [[Guggenheim Fellowship]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.gf.org/fellows/results?competition=ALL&fellowship_category=ALL&lower_bound=1996&page=4&query=&upper_bound=1996&x=26&y=11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121002224321/http://www.gf.org/fellows/results?competition=ALL&fellowship_category=ALL&lower_bound=1996&page=4&query=&upper_bound=1996&x=26&y=11|url-status=dead|archive-date=2012-10-02|title=Search Results - John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|date=2012-10-02|access-date=2018-04-24}}</ref>
*1979-1983 - [[National Institutes of Health]] Research Career Development Award
*1981-1983 - [[Alfred P. Sloan]] Fellowship

== Patents ==
Wightman holds two patents through the [[United States Patent and Trademark Office]], patents 4,038,158 and 4,041,346. Both [[patents]] are listed under the name: electrochemical generation of field desorption emitters.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://pdfpiw.uspto.gov/.piw?Docid=4038158&idkey=NONE&homeurl=http:%252F%252Fpatft.uspto.gov%252Fnetahtml%252FPTO%252Fpatimg.htm|title=Patent Images|website=pdfpiw.uspto.gov|access-date=2018-04-24}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://pdfpiw.uspto.gov/.piw?Docid=4041346&idkey=NONE&homeurl=http:%252F%252Fpatft.uspto.gov%252Fnetahtml%252FPTO%252Fpatimg.htm|title=Patent Images|website=pdfpiw.uspto.gov|access-date=2018-04-24}}</ref>
